explanations.explanation: That's the offer, baker. The LORD says, “…then I will forgive the city.” Notice who gets the benefit: the whole city, not just the one person who gets found. One honest soul on the streets, and Jerusalem is forgiven. That's a door left wide open.

I like the thinking, but the verse never hands out a promotion. No robe, no gavel, no office. The LORD says, “…then I will forgive the city.” The reward goes to the whole city, and the person who gets found doesn't even get a thank-you card.

Nobody's calling a construction crew in this verse. The LORD's promise is, “…then I will forgive the city.” Forgiveness is what's on the table, not bricks and mortar. I'd bring a trowel anyway, though. That's just me.

I get why you'd pick it, since the words sound right. But verse 2 says, “Although they say, ‘As surely as the LORD lives,’ they are swearing falsely.” They say the right words, and the oath is still false. Saying a thing and meaning it are two different batches.

That's it. The text says, “Although they say, ‘As surely as the LORD lives,’ they are swearing falsely.” The words are in their mouths, and the oath is false anyway. A stamp can press a perfect word into dough, but that doesn't mean the cookie is any good.

Yes, baker. Verse 3 says, “They have made their faces harder than stone and refused to repent.” The LORD struck them and they felt no pain. He finished them off, and they refused to accept discipline. That's a lot of hard chances turned down.

Close, but that isn't the word. Verse 3 says they felt no pain when the LORD struck them, so mourning isn't what the text reports. What it says is that they “refused to repent.” Repenting means turning around, and that's the thing they wouldn't do.
Plenty of us would complain, but the text doesn't say it here. Verse 3 says the people “refused to repent.” Nobody in the verse is filing a complaint. They're just not turning back.

That's right. The speaker says, “I will go to the powerful and speak to them. Surely they know the way of the LORD, the justice of their God.” He'd just called the poor fools who don't know the way of the LORD, so he figures the people at the top must do better. He's about to find out.

Farmers are a good guess in a vineyard-and-harvest sort of book, but they aren't named here. The speaker says, “I will go to the powerful and speak to them.” The powerful are the ones he's counting on to know the way of the LORD.

Widows don't come up in these verses. Right after talking about the poor, the speaker says he'll go to the powerful. His thinking is that surely they know the way of the LORD, the justice of their God.

That's what the speaker was hoping for, baker. He said, “Surely they know the way of the LORD.” Then the text says, “But they too, with one accord, had broken the yoke and torn off the chains.” The powerful don't keep the way of the LORD. They did the very opposite.

Right. The speaker expected better from them, but verse 5 says, “But they too, with one accord, had broken the yoke and torn off the chains.” So the powerful aren't keeping the way of the LORD. It's the same story at the top as it was lower down.

Yes. Verse 6 says why: “For their rebellious acts are many, and their unfaithful deeds are numerous.” A lion, a wolf and a leopard sound like a zoo trip nobody signed up for. The text gives the reason plainly, and it's what the people have done.

The verse never mentions fallen walls. It names a lion, a wolf and a leopard, and then gives the reason: “For their rebellious acts are many, and their unfaithful deeds are numerous.” The trouble comes because of what they did, not because of their walls.

Shepherds aren't in this verse at all. The reason it gives is, “For their rebellious acts are many, and their unfaithful deeds are numerous.” Those are the people's own deeds, and the verse says no more than that.

That's it. Verse 7 says, “Your children have forsaken Me and sworn by gods that are not gods.” Back in verse 2 they were swearing falsely by the LORD's name. Now the LORD says they've sworn by gods that aren't gods.
I can see why that sounds like an oath, but the text doesn't say it. Verse 7 says they “sworn by gods that are not gods.” Gold isn't mentioned at all.
A king sounds like a believable pick, baker, but he's not in this verse. The LORD says they “sworn by gods that are not gods.” That's what they swore by instead of Him.

Yes. The LORD says, “I satisfied their needs, yet they committed adultery and assembled at the houses of prostitutes.” He took care of them, and they still went away from Him. This one is heavy, and I think it hurts to read.
The text says the opposite. In verse 7 the LORD says, “I satisfied their needs.” That's the very thing He puts before the word “yet.” It's a heavy verse, and I think it hurts to read.

That's the question. The LORD says, “Should I not punish them for these things?” and then asks again, “Should I not avenge Myself on such a nation as this?” He's just listed what they've done, and now He asks about it. This part is heavy, baker, so take a breath.
It's a hopeful question, but it's not the one the LORD asks here. After the list, He says, “Should I not punish them for these things?” That's the question in verse 9.
Nobody pleads in this verse. Right after listing what they've done, the LORD asks, “Should I not punish them for these things?” That's the question that follows.
Yes. The LORD says, “Go up through her vineyards and ravage them, but do not finish them off.” There's a limit set right inside the order. The damage comes with a line it must not cross.
That would be a clever limit, but the verse doesn't give it. The order is to ravage the vineyards, “but do not finish them off.” Vines aren't sorted by age anywhere in the text.
No timing is given here. The LORD says to go up through the vineyards and ravage them, “but do not finish them off.” That's the only limit in the verse.

explanations.answer: They do not belong to the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the reason. The LORD says, “Strip off her branches, for they do not belong to the LORD.” The text gives no other reason, so we don't add one.
It sounds like a reasonable cause, but the verse doesn't say it. The LORD's reason is, “…for they do not belong to the LORD.” The branches are stripped because they aren't His.
Wild vines would be a good guess for a vineyard, baker. But the text says, “Strip off her branches, for they do not belong to the LORD.” That's the whole reason it gives.

Yes. The LORD says, “For the house of Israel and the house of Judah have been utterly unfaithful to Me.” Both houses are named, and the word is “utterly.” That's a heavy thing to say about both of them.
The text says both. The LORD declares, “For the house of Israel and the house of Judah have been utterly unfaithful to Me.” Neither house is left out. It's a hard verse, but it's what the text says.
That's what they say. Verse 12 says they lied about the LORD and said, “He will not do anything; harm will not come to us; we will not see sword or famine.” They've decided He's not going to act.
Offerings aren't in this verse at all. What the people say is, “He will not do anything; harm will not come to us; we will not see sword or famine.” That's the lie they tell about the LORD.
That sounds like a dramatic thing to say, but it's not what the verse has them say. They say, “He will not do anything.” They also say no harm, no sword and no famine will come to them.

I see why you'd lean that way, but the text goes the other direction. In verse 13 the people say, “The prophets are but wind, for the word is not in them.” They don't think the prophets carry the LORD's word. They say it isn't in them.

Right. The people say, “The prophets are but wind, for the word is not in them.” That's the opposite of believing the prophets carry the LORD's word. They brush the prophets off and say their predictions can fall on themselves.

Yes. The LORD says, “I will make My words a fire in your mouth and this people the wood it consumes.” They called the prophets wind, and He answers with fire. Wind and fire, baker. Those are the words, right there.
Flood sounds like a believable pick, but it's not the word. The LORD says, “I will make My words a fire in your mouth.” A fire needs wood, and He says this people are the wood.
A storm fits with all that wind talk, I'll give you that. But the LORD says, “I will make My words a fire in your mouth and this people the wood it consumes.” Fire is what He names.

explanations.answer: The people won't know its language
explanations.explanation: That's right. The LORD calls it “a nation whose language you do not know and whose speech you do not understand.” Imagine a nation showing up, and you can't make out a single word they say. It's one more way the LORD says they will be strangers to His people.

The verse doesn't tell us how they'll arrive. It says this nation is distant, established and ancient, and that it's “a nation whose language you do not know and whose speech you do not understand.” The sea isn't mentioned.
The text points the other way. Verse 16 says, “they are all mighty men.” About this nation, verse 15 also says the people won't understand its speech.

The people may have counted on those cities, but the text says otherwise. Verse 17 says, “With the sword they will destroy the fortified cities in which you trust.” The cities don't hold. It's a heavy verse, so take it slowly.

Right. The LORD says, “With the sword they will destroy the fortified cities in which you trust.” The cities don't hold off this nation. Notice that the people trusted in them. It's a heavy verse, and I think it's hard to read.
Yes. The LORD says, “Just as you have forsaken Me and served foreign gods in your land…” That's the first blank. It's the answer to the people's question about what offense they committed.

That's the second blank. The LORD says, “…so will you serve foreigners in a land that is not your own.” They served foreign gods in their own land, and now they will serve foreigners in a land that isn't theirs. The two halves of the sentence line up.

Prophets did come up earlier, in verse 13, when the people called them wind. But the LORD's answer in verse 19 doesn't say they served foreign prophets. It says they “served foreign gods in your land.”

Shepherds aren't in this passage's answer at all. The LORD says, “Just as you have forsaken Me and served foreign gods in your land, so will you serve foreigners in a land that is not your own.” The words that fit are gods and foreigners.
Neighbors came up in verse 8, when the LORD talked about a neighbor's wife. That's a different thing from this answer. In verse 19 He says the people served foreign gods and will serve foreigners.
